title: Anatomy & Physiology I
summary: The first semester of college A&P, in syllabus order: body organization and homeostasis, chemistry, cells, tissues, skin, bones, muscles, and the nervous system. Built around the structures the lab practical asks you to name and the mechanisms the lecture exam asks you to explain.

lessons.title: Organization of the body and homeostasis
lessons.body:
A&P starts with a map. Anatomy asks *what is it and where is it*; physiology asks *what does it do and how*. The course keeps looping back to one idea: **structure predicts function**. A flat sheet of cells is built for diffusion; a thick barrel of muscle is built for force.

## Levels of organization

Chemical, then cellular, then tissue, then organ, then organ system, then organism. Eleven organ systems: integumentary, skeletal, muscular, nervous, endocrine, cardiovascular, lymphatic, respiratory, digestive, urinary, reproductive. Semester I covers the first four in depth.

## Homeostasis and feedback

Homeostasis is keeping internal conditions inside a narrow survivable range while the outside world swings. Every loop has the same three parts: a **receptor** that senses, a **control center** (usually hypothalamus, brainstem, or an endocrine gland) that compares the reading to a set point, and an **effector** that changes something.

**Negative feedback** reverses the change and is the rule — body temperature near `37 C`, blood glucose near `90 mg/dL`, arterial pH `7.35–7.45`. Get cold, you shiver and constrict skin vessels; get hot, you sweat and dilate them. **Positive feedback** amplifies the change until an endpoint ends it: oxytocin in labor, the platelet plug in clotting, and the sodium influx that fires an action potential.

> **Trap:** Positive feedback is not "good" feedback and negative is not "bad." The sign describes the direction of the response, not its value.

## Anatomical position and directional terms

All direction words assume **anatomical position**: standing, feet forward, arms at the sides, palms facing forward. Superior/inferior, anterior (ventral)/posterior (dorsal), medial/lateral, proximal/distal (limbs only), superficial/deep. The elbow is proximal to the wrist; the sternum is medial to the nipple.

## Planes

- **Sagittal** divides left and right; **midsagittal** splits them evenly.
- **Frontal (coronal)** divides anterior from posterior.
- **Transverse (horizontal, cross section)** divides superior from inferior.
- **Oblique** is any angled cut.

## Cavities and membranes

The **dorsal cavity** holds the cranial cavity (brain) and vertebral canal (spinal cord). The **ventral cavity** splits at the diaphragm into the **thoracic** cavity — two pleural cavities plus the mediastinum, which contains the pericardial cavity — and the **abdominopelvic** cavity.

Serous membranes come in pairs: **parietal** lines the wall, **visceral** hugs the organ, and serous fluid between them lets surfaces slide. Pleura, pericardium, peritoneum. Organs behind the peritoneum — kidneys, pancreas, most of the duodenum, abdominal aorta — are **retroperitoneal**.

## Regions and quadrants

Clinically the abdomen is four quadrants (RUQ, LUQ, RLQ, LLQ). Anatomically it is nine regions: right/left hypochondriac and epigastric on top, right/left lumbar and umbilical in the middle, right/left iliac (inguinal) and hypogastric below. Surface regions you must name: brachial (arm), antecubital (front of elbow), carpal (wrist), popliteal (back of knee), sural (calf), cervical (neck), axillary (armpit), inguinal (groin), gluteal, occipital.

> **Key:** Every lab practical question is really "name it and place it." Learn the term, the plain-English location, and the plane you would cut to see it.
keyPoints: Structure predicts function — the shape of a tissue tells you its job.
Every feedback loop is receptor, control center, effector; negative feedback reverses change, positive amplifies it.
Directional terms only make sense from anatomical position: standing, palms forward.
Serous membranes are paired: parietal lines the cavity, visceral covers the organ.
Retroperitoneal organs include the kidneys, pancreas, and abdominal aorta.

checks.q: A midsagittal cut through the body produces which two pieces?
checks.why: Sagittal planes divide left from right; midsagittal divides them equally. Frontal separates anterior from posterior, transverse separates superior from inferior.

checks.q: Oxytocin release during labor rising until the baby is delivered is an example of:
checks.why: The response amplifies the original stimulus (more stretch to more oxytocin to more stretch) until delivery ends the loop. Negative feedback would reduce contractions.

checks.q: Which organ is retroperitoneal?
checks.why: Kidneys sit behind the parietal peritoneum, as do the pancreas, duodenum and abdominal aorta. Stomach, spleen and transverse colon are intraperitoneal.

lessons.title: The chemistry A&P actually uses
lessons.body:
You do not need general chemistry to pass A&P, but you need the handful of chemical ideas that physiology runs on: bonds, water, pH, and the four organic molecules.

## Atoms and bonds

Atomic number is protons; mass number is protons plus neutrons; isotopes differ only in neutrons. Four elements make up about `96%` of body mass: oxygen `65%`, carbon `18%`, hydrogen `10%`, nitrogen `3%`. Trace but essential: calcium, phosphorus, potassium, sodium, chloride, magnesium, iron, iodine.

- **Ionic bonds** transfer electrons. `NaCl` dissociates in water into `Na+` and `Cl-`. Ions that conduct current in solution are **electrolytes**.
- **Covalent bonds** share electrons. Equal sharing is nonpolar (fats, `O2`); unequal sharing is polar (water).
- **Hydrogen bonds** are weak attractions between a partially positive H and a partially negative O or N. Individually trivial, collectively they hold DNA's strands together and give proteins their shape.

## Why water matters

Water is `50–60%` of adult body weight and it is polar, so it dissolves ions and other polar molecules (**hydrophilic**) and refuses fats (**hydrophobic**). That single fact builds the cell membrane and drives protein folding. Water also has high heat capacity, so body temperature changes slowly, and high heat of vaporization, so sweat carries away large heat for small volume.

Water participates in reactions directly. **Dehydration synthesis** removes a water molecule to join two monomers; **hydrolysis** adds water to split a polymer. Digestion is hydrolysis from mouth to ileum.

## Acids, bases, buffers

pH is a measure of hydrogen ion concentration on a log scale, so a drop of one pH unit is a tenfold rise in `H+`. Blood is held at `7.35–7.45`; below `7.35` is acidemia, above `7.45` alkalemia, and outside roughly `6.8–7.8` proteins denature and you die.

The main blood buffer is the **bicarbonate system**: `CO2 + H2O <-> H2CO3 <-> H+ + HCO3-`. Blow off `CO2` and pH rises; retain it and pH falls. This is why the lungs are a pH organ, a point A&P II will hammer.

> **Key:** Buffers act in seconds, the lungs in minutes, the kidneys in hours to days.

## The four organic molecules

| Class | Monomer | Body jobs |
|---|---|---|
| Carbohydrate | Monosaccharide (glucose) | Fast fuel; glycogen storage in liver and muscle |
| Lipid | Fatty acid + glycerol | Dense energy `9 kcal/g`, membranes (phospholipids), steroid hormones from cholesterol |
| Protein | Amino acid (20 kinds) | Enzymes, transporters, channels, contraction, antibodies, structure |
| Nucleic acid | Nucleotide | DNA stores the code, RNA carries and reads it, ATP moves energy |

Protein structure runs primary (sequence), secondary (alpha helix, beta sheet, held by hydrogen bonds), tertiary (3-D fold), quaternary (multiple chains, as in hemoglobin's four). Heat, extreme pH, or heavy metals **denature** a protein — the fold unravels and function stops, which is why a fever of `41 C` is dangerous.

Enzymes are protein catalysts that lower activation energy without being consumed. They are specific (active site fits one substrate shape), saturable, and sensitive to pH and temperature — pepsin works at `pH 2`, pancreatic enzymes at `pH 8`.

> **Trap:** ATP does not "contain" energy like a battery cell. The energy is released when the terminal phosphate bond is hydrolyzed, yielding ADP plus inorganic phosphate.
keyPoints: Oxygen, carbon, hydrogen and nitrogen make up about 96% of body mass.
Dehydration synthesis builds polymers, hydrolysis breaks them — digestion is hydrolysis.
Blood pH is 7.35–7.45; the bicarbonate buffer plus the lungs and kidneys defend it.
Four organic classes: carbohydrate, lipid, protein, nucleic acid.
Enzymes lower activation energy, are substrate-specific, and denature with heat or extreme pH.

checks.q: Two amino acids join and a water molecule is released. This reaction is:
checks.why: Removing water to link monomers is dehydration synthesis. Hydrolysis is the reverse — adding water to split a bond, which is what digestion does.

checks.q: Which bond type holds the two strands of DNA together and stabilizes the alpha helix of a protein?
checks.why: Hydrogen bonds are individually weak but numerous, which lets DNA unzip for replication. Peptide bonds are the covalent links of primary structure, not the helix stabilizer.

checks.q: A patient hypoventilates and retains carbon dioxide. Using the bicarbonate equation, blood pH will:
choices: Rise, because CO2 is a base
Fall, because more CO2 drives H+ production
Stay the same, because buffers are infinite
checks.why: CO2 plus water forms carbonic acid, which dissociates to H+ and bicarbonate. More CO2 means more free H+ and a lower pH. Buffers blunt the change but do not erase it.

lessons.title: The cell: membranes, transport, and protein synthesis
lessons.body:
## The membrane

The plasma membrane is a **phospholipid bilayer**: phosphate heads facing water, fatty acid tails facing each other. That arrangement means small nonpolar things (`O2`, `CO2`, steroids) cross freely and ions, glucose and water need help. Cholesterol wedged between the tails keeps the membrane fluid at cold temperature and stable at warm. Membrane proteins act as channels, carriers, pumps, receptors, enzymes, and identity markers (glycoproteins of the glycocalyx).

## Passive transport — no ATP

- **Simple diffusion**: down a concentration gradient, straight through the lipid. Gas exchange in the lung.
- **Facilitated diffusion**: down a gradient but through a channel or carrier. `GLUT4` moving glucose into muscle.
- **Osmosis**: water moving to the side with more solute, through aquaporins. Tonicity describes what a solution does to a cell — **isotonic** (`0.9% NaCl`) leaves it alone, **hypotonic** swells and can lyse it, **hypertonic** shrivels (crenates) it.
- **Filtration**: hydrostatic pressure pushes water and solutes across, as in the glomerulus.

## Active transport — ATP required

**Primary active transport** burns ATP directly. The star is the **sodium-potassium pump (Na+/K+ ATPase)**: three `Na+` out, two `K+` in, per ATP. It runs constantly, consumes a large share of resting energy, and creates the gradients everything else borrows.

**Secondary active transport** uses the sodium gradient rather than ATP itself — the `SGLT` cotransporter drags glucose into intestinal and kidney cells alongside sodium.

**Bulk transport** moves large cargo in vesicles: endocytosis (phagocytosis for solids, pinocytosis for fluid, receptor-mediated for specific ligands like LDL) and exocytosis for secretion.

## Resting membrane potential

Every cell is electrically negative inside, typically `-70 mV` in a neuron and about `-90 mV` in skeletal muscle. Three facts explain it: potassium is concentrated inside and leaks out through more open leak channels than sodium has; large anionic proteins trapped inside cannot follow; and the `Na+/K+` pump exports one more positive charge than it imports.

> **Key:** Potassium sets the resting potential. Sodium creates the action potential. That one sentence explains why a rising serum potassium destabilizes the heart.

## Organelles worth naming

Nucleus (DNA, nucleolus makes ribosomes), rough ER (protein synthesis, studded with ribosomes), smooth ER (lipid and steroid synthesis, detox, calcium storage), Golgi apparatus (modifies, sorts, ships), mitochondria (ATP by aerobic respiration, own DNA, maternally inherited), lysosomes (acid hydrolases, digest), peroxisomes (neutralize free radicals), cytoskeleton (microfilaments, intermediate filaments, microtubules), centrioles (spindle), cilia (move fluid), flagellum (sperm).

## Protein synthesis

**Transcription** happens in the nucleus: RNA polymerase copies one DNA strand into pre-mRNA, introns are spliced out, exons stay. **Translation** happens on a ribosome: mRNA is read in three-base **codons**, each tRNA brings the matching amino acid through its anticodon, and peptide bonds link them. Start codon `AUG` (methionine); stop codons `UAA`, `UAG`, `UGA`. There are `64` codons for `20` amino acids, so the code is redundant.

Proteins destined for secretion or membranes are made on rough ER, packaged by Golgi, and exported by exocytosis. Cytosolic proteins are made on free ribosomes.

## Cell cycle

Interphase is `G1` (growth), `S` (DNA replication), `G2` (prep). Mitosis is prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase, then cytokinesis. Checkpoints stop a damaged cell from dividing; losing them is the root of cancer.

> **Trap:** Mitosis produces two genetically identical diploid cells. Meiosis, which only gametes do, produces four haploid cells and shuffles the genes.
keyPoints: The Na+/K+ ATPase pumps 3 Na+ out for 2 K+ in per ATP and builds the gradients everything else uses.
Resting potential is about -70 mV in a neuron; potassium leak sets it.
Isotonic saline is 0.9% NaCl; hypotonic swells cells, hypertonic shrinks them.
Transcription is DNA to mRNA in the nucleus; translation is mRNA to protein on the ribosome.
Start codon AUG; stop codons UAA, UAG, UGA; 64 codons for 20 amino acids.

checks.q: A red blood cell is placed in distilled water. What happens and why?
choices: It shrinks, because water leaves down its gradient
It swells and may lyse, because water enters the more concentrated cell
Nothing, because the membrane is impermeable to water
It shrinks, because sodium pumps stop
checks.why: Distilled water is hypotonic, so water moves into the solute-rich cytoplasm through aquaporins until the cell bursts. Shrinkage happens in hypertonic solution.

checks.q: Glucose entering an intestinal cell alongside sodium, using the sodium gradient rather than ATP directly, is:
checks.why: Secondary active transport spends the stored sodium gradient, which the ATP-driven pump created. Primary active transport hydrolyzes ATP at the transporter itself.

checks.q: A drug blocks the rough endoplasmic reticulum. Which product is most affected?
choices: A hormone secreted from the cell
checks.why: Secreted and membrane proteins are made on rough ER. ATP is mitochondrial, steroids are smooth ER, and peroxisomes handle free radicals.

lessons.title: Histology: the four tissue types
lessons.body:
Histology is the part of A&P I where the lab practical is pure pattern recognition — you look down a scope and name what you see. Four tissue types: epithelial, connective, muscle, nervous.

## Epithelial tissue

Covers surfaces, lines cavities, forms glands. Five shared traits: cells are packed with little matrix, it sits on a **basement membrane**, it has a free **apical** surface and an attached **basal** surface, it is **avascular** (fed by diffusion from below) and it regenerates fast.

Name it twice: layers then shape.

| Type | Where | Why there |
|---|---|---|
| Simple squamous | Alveoli, capillary endothelium, serous membranes | Thin, for diffusion and filtration |
| Simple cuboidal | Kidney tubules, gland ducts, thyroid follicles | Secretion and absorption |
| Simple columnar | Stomach, intestine (with microvilli and goblet cells) | Absorption and mucus |
| Pseudostratified ciliated columnar | Trachea, bronchi | Sweeps mucus upward |
| Stratified squamous | Epidermis (keratinized), esophagus, vagina (non-keratinized) | Takes abrasion |
| Transitional (urothelium) | Bladder, ureters | Stretches without tearing |

Glands are **endocrine** (ductless, into blood) or **exocrine** (duct, onto a surface). Exocrine secretion modes: merocrine (exocytosis, sweat and pancreas), apocrine (pinches off apex), holocrine (cell ruptures, sebaceous glands).

## Connective tissue

The opposite build: few cells, lots of **extracellular matrix** — ground substance plus fibers. Fibers are **collagen** (strong, ropey), **elastic** (recoils), and **reticular** (fine mesh scaffolding). Most connective tissue is well vascularized; cartilage is the exception.

- **Loose areolar**: the packing material under epithelia, holds fluid.
- **Adipose**: fat storage, insulation, cushion.
- **Reticular**: framework of lymph nodes, spleen, bone marrow.
- **Dense regular**: parallel collagen — tendons and ligaments.
- **Dense irregular**: collagen in all directions — dermis, organ capsules.
- **Cartilage**: chondrocytes in lacunae, avascular so it heals slowly. Hyaline (most common; costal cartilage, articular surfaces, fetal skeleton), elastic (ear, epiglottis), fibrocartilage (intervertebral discs, pubic symphysis, knee menisci).
- **Bone**: hard matrix of collagen plus calcium phosphate.
- **Blood**: cells in a liquid matrix (plasma). It counts because it comes from mesenchyme.

> **Trap:** "Avascular" is the reason a torn meniscus or ligament heals badly while a cut lip heals in days.

## Muscle tissue

| | Skeletal | Cardiac | Smooth |
|---|---|---|---|
| Striations | Yes | Yes | No |
| Nuclei | Many, peripheral | One or two, central | One, central |
| Control | Voluntary | Involuntary | Involuntary |
| Special | Attaches to bone | Intercalated discs, gap junctions | Sheets, peristalsis |

## Nervous tissue

Neurons (excitable, conduct signals) plus neuroglia (support, far more numerous). Covered in detail later.

## Membranes and repair

Tissue membranes: **mucous** (lines cavities open to the outside, always wet), **serous** (closed cavities, parietal and visceral layers), **cutaneous** (the skin, dry), **synovial** (joint cavities, no epithelium at all).

Repair happens by **regeneration** (same tissue back — epithelium, bone, liver) or **fibrosis** (scar collagen — cardiac muscle, CNS, deep burns). Which one you get depends on tissue type and depth of injury.

> **On the exam:** Given a slide description, first decide "lots of cells or lots of matrix?" That one question separates epithelium from connective tissue before you look at anything else.
keyPoints: Epithelium is avascular, polarized, sits on a basement membrane, and is named by layers then cell shape.
Connective tissue is defined by its extracellular matrix; collagen is strength, elastic is recoil.
Hyaline cartilage is the most common; fibrocartilage takes compression in discs and menisci.
Skeletal muscle is striated and multinucleate; cardiac has intercalated discs; smooth has neither.
Cardiac muscle and CNS tissue heal by fibrosis, not regeneration.

checks.q: A slide shows a single layer of flattened cells forming a wall one cell thick. Where does this tissue most likely come from?
checks.why: Simple squamous epithelium is built for rapid diffusion, which is exactly the alveolar wall. Bladder is transitional, palm is thick keratinized stratified squamous, tendon is dense regular connective tissue.

checks.q: Why does a torn meniscus heal poorly compared with a skin laceration?
checks.why: Cartilage has no blood supply, so nutrients and repair cells arrive only by slow diffusion. Skin epithelium is fed from a vascular dermis and regenerates quickly.

checks.q: Intercalated discs identify which tissue?
checks.why: Intercalated discs contain desmosomes and gap junctions that let cardiac cells contract as one unit. Skeletal muscle is striated but has no discs; smooth muscle has neither.

lessons.title: The integumentary system
lessons.body:
The skin is the largest organ — about `1.5–2.0 m2` and `7%` of body weight — and it is a legitimate organ because it contains all four tissue types.

## Layers

**Epidermis**: keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, avascular. From deep to superficial, the layers are stratum **basale**, **spinosum**, **granulosum**, **lucidum** (thick skin of palms and soles only), and **corneum**. Cells are born by mitosis in the basale, fill with keratin as they push up, die, and flake off in `25–45` days.

Four epidermal cells: **keratinocytes** (the bulk, make keratin), **melanocytes** (in the basale, make melanin and hand it to keratinocytes as a UV umbrella), **Langerhans (dendritic) cells** (immune sentries), **Merkel cells** (light touch).

Skin color comes from melanin (brown to black), carotene (yellow-orange, from diet), and hemoglobin showing through (pink). Everyone has roughly the same number of melanocytes; the difference is how much melanin they make.

**Dermis**: dense connective tissue with the blood supply, nerves, and glands. The **papillary layer** is loose areolar with dermal papillae that form fingerprints and carry capillaries and Meissner corpuscles. The **reticular layer** is dense irregular collagen and elastin — the `80%` of the dermis that gives skin its toughness and, when it tears from rapid stretch, makes stretch marks.

**Hypodermis (subcutaneous layer)** is not technically skin: areolar and adipose tissue that anchors skin, insulates, and is where subcutaneous injections go.

## Accessory structures

- **Hair**: shaft above the surface, root below, grown by the matrix in the bulb. **Arrector pili** smooth muscle makes goosebumps.
- **Nails**: hard keratin. Nail matrix grows it; the pale lunula is the thick matrix showing through.
- **Sweat glands**: **eccrine (merocrine)** open onto the skin everywhere, secrete watery sweat for thermoregulation. **Apocrine** open into hair follicles in the axilla and groin, activate at puberty, and their secretion feeds odor-making bacteria. **Ceruminous** glands make earwax; mammary glands make milk.
- **Sebaceous glands**: holocrine, oil (sebum) into the follicle, keeps skin and hair pliable and mildly antibacterial. Blocked and infected, that is acne.

## Functions

Protection (physical, chemical acid mantle `pH 4–6`, biological), **thermoregulation** (sweat plus dermal vessel dilation or constriction), **sensation**, **vitamin D synthesis** (UVB converts a cholesterol derivative in the epidermis to cholecalciferol, finished by liver and kidney), **excretion** of small amounts of nitrogenous waste, and **blood reservoir** — the dermis can hold `5%` of blood volume and shunt it out when needed.

## Burns

| Depth | Involves | Looks like |
|---|---|---|
| Superficial (1st degree) | Epidermis | Red, painful, no blister; heals in `3–5` days |
| Partial thickness (2nd) | Epidermis plus part of dermis | Blisters, very painful, blanches |
| Full thickness (3rd) | Entire dermis, may reach fat | White/leathery/charred, painless in the center, needs grafting |

Surface area is estimated with the **rule of nines** in adults: head `9%`, each arm `9%`, each leg `18%`, anterior trunk `18%`, posterior trunk `18%`, perineum `1%`. The dangers are fluid loss, infection, and hypothermia, not the wound itself.

> **Key:** A full-thickness burn is painless in the center because the sensory nerve endings in the dermis were destroyed. Painless is worse, not better.

## Healing and skin cancer

Healing runs inflammation, then proliferation with granulation tissue, then remodeling over weeks to a year. Skin cancers: **basal cell carcinoma** (most common, least dangerous, stratum basale), **squamous cell carcinoma** (stratum spinosum, can metastasize), **melanoma** (melanocytes, most lethal). Screen with **ABCDE**: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color variation, Diameter over `6 mm`, Evolving.
keyPoints: Epidermal layers deep to superficial: basale, spinosum, granulosum, lucidum (thick skin only), corneum.
Melanocytes live in the stratum basale; melanin count differs, melanocyte number does not.
The reticular dermis is dense irregular connective tissue and supplies the skin's strength.
Eccrine sweat is thermoregulatory; apocrine sweat is puberty-onset and odor-related.
Rule of nines in adults: head 9, each arm 9, each leg 18, each trunk surface 18, perineum 1.

checks.q: In which epidermal layer does mitosis occur?
checks.why: The basale sits on the basement membrane next to the dermal blood supply, so it is the only layer nourished enough to divide. The corneum is dead, flattened cells.

checks.q: A burn is white and leathery, and the patient reports no pain in the center of the wound. This describes:
checks.why: Full thickness destroys the dermis, taking the sensory receptors with it. Superficial and partial thickness burns preserve nerve endings and hurt sharply.

checks.q: Sebaceous glands release their product by:
checks.why: Sebaceous cells fill with sebum and burst, so the cell itself becomes the secretion. Eccrine sweat glands are the classic merocrine example.

lessons.title: Bone tissue: histology, growth, remodeling, and calcium
lessons.body:
Bone is connective tissue with a mineralized matrix — about one-third collagen (flexible, resists tension) and two-thirds hydroxyapatite calcium phosphate (rigid, resists compression). Lose the collagen and bone shatters like chalk; lose the mineral and it bends like rubber.

## Functions

Support, protection, movement (levers for muscle), mineral storage (`99%` of body calcium, plus phosphate), blood cell formation (red marrow), and triglyceride storage (yellow marrow).

## Gross anatomy of a long bone

**Diaphysis** is the shaft of compact bone around a medullary cavity. **Epiphyses** are the ends: spongy bone inside, **articular cartilage** (hyaline) outside where the joint is. The **metaphysis** between them contains the **epiphyseal plate** in a growing bone and the epiphyseal line once growth ends. **Periosteum** covers the outside (osteogenic inner layer, fibrous outer, anchored by Sharpey fibers); **endosteum** lines the inside.

## Microscopic structure

Compact bone is built of **osteons (Haversian systems)**: concentric lamellae of matrix around a **central (Haversian) canal** carrying vessels and nerves. **Osteocytes** sit in **lacunae** and talk to each other through **canaliculi**. **Perforating (Volkmann) canals** run crosswise, linking central canals to periosteum. Spongy bone has no osteons — it is a lattice of **trabeculae** aligned along lines of stress, with marrow in the spaces.

Four bone cells:

- **Osteogenic (osteoprogenitor)**: stem cells in periosteum and endosteum.
- **Osteoblasts**: build matrix (osteoid), then get trapped.
- **Osteocytes**: mature, maintain matrix, sense mechanical strain.
- **Osteoclasts**: huge multinucleate cells from monocyte lineage; they resorb bone with acid and enzymes in a ruffled border.

> **Key:** blasts Build, clasts Consume. Every question about bone balance is a question about which one is winning.

## Ossification

**Intramembranous ossification** builds flat bones — skull, clavicle — directly inside a fibrous membrane. **Endochondral ossification** builds everything else by replacing a hyaline cartilage model, starting at the primary ossification center in the diaphysis and later at secondary centers in the epiphyses.

Length comes from the **epiphyseal plate**, which has five zones: resting, proliferation, hypertrophy, calcification, ossification. Cartilage is added on the epiphyseal side and replaced by bone on the diaphyseal side, so the bone lengthens while the plate stays the same thickness. It closes at roughly `18` in females and `21` in males, and after that no one gets taller. Width comes from **appositional growth** — osteoblasts under the periosteum add bone outside while osteoclasts widen the medullary cavity inside.

## Remodeling and repair

About `5–10%` of the skeleton is replaced yearly. **Wolff's law**: bone remodels along the lines of stress it experiences, which is why loaded bone thickens and bedrest or spaceflight thins it.

Fracture repair: hematoma forms, then a fibrocartilaginous (soft) callus, then a bony (hard) callus in `6–8` weeks, then remodeling over months.

## Calcium regulation

Blood calcium is defended tightly at about `9.0–10.5 mg/dL` because nerves and muscle depend on it.

- **Parathyroid hormone (PTH)** rises when calcium falls. It activates osteoclasts, increases kidney calcium reabsorption, increases phosphate excretion, and activates vitamin D to raise gut absorption. Net: calcium up.
- **Calcitonin** from thyroid C cells inhibits osteoclasts. Net: calcium down. Its role in adult humans is minor — exam answers still expect it as PTH's opposite.
- **Calcitriol** (active vitamin D) is the gut absorption hormone.

Low calcium causes tetany and hyperexcitable nerves; high calcium causes lethargy, weak muscles, and stones.

> **Trap:** Osteoporosis is normal mineral in too little bone; osteomalacia and rickets are too little mineral in normal bone volume, usually from vitamin D deficiency.
keyPoints: Bone matrix is collagen for tension plus hydroxyapatite for compression.
Osteoblasts build, osteoclasts resorb, osteocytes maintain and sense strain.
The osteon with its central canal is the unit of compact bone; spongy bone has trabeculae instead.
Length comes from the epiphyseal plate, width from appositional growth under the periosteum.
PTH raises blood calcium by activating osteoclasts, kidney reabsorption and vitamin D; calcitonin opposes it.

checks.q: Blood calcium falls to 7.8 mg/dL. The expected response is:
choices: PTH release and increased urinary calcium loss
checks.why: Low calcium triggers PTH, which frees calcium from bone, retains it in the kidney, and activates vitamin D for gut uptake. Calcitonin does the opposite and would worsen the problem.

checks.q: A 12-year-old fractures the distal femur through the epiphyseal plate. The main long-term concern is:
choices: Growth in length may be disrupted
checks.why: The epiphyseal plate is the engine of lengthwise growth, so damaging it can shorten or angle the limb. Appositional widening under the periosteum is a separate process.

checks.q: Astronauts lose bone density in microgravity. This best illustrates:
checks.why: Wolff's law says bone remodels to match mechanical stress; remove the load and osteoclasts outpace osteoblasts. It is a remodeling phenomenon, not a growth-plate or feedback one.

lessons.title: The skeleton by name, and how joints move
lessons.body:
There are `206` bones in the adult: `80` axial and `126` appendicular. The lab practical asks you to point at a bone and name the landmark, so learn the bone and its bumps together.

## Axial skeleton

**Skull — 8 cranial bones**: frontal, two parietal, two temporal, occipital, sphenoid, ethmoid. Landmarks: **foramen magnum** (occipital, where the cord exits), **sella turcica** (sphenoid, holds the pituitary), **cribriform plate** (ethmoid, olfactory nerve fibers), **mastoid** and **styloid processes** and the **external acoustic meatus** (temporal). Sutures: coronal, sagittal, lambdoid, squamous.

**14 facial bones**: two maxillae, two zygomatic, two nasal, two lacrimal, two palatine, two inferior nasal conchae, vomer, mandible. The mandible is the only freely movable skull bone; its condyle meets the temporal bone at the TMJ. Paranasal sinuses sit in the frontal, sphenoid, ethmoid, and maxillary bones.

**Vertebral column — 26 bones**: `7` cervical, `12` thoracic, `5` lumbar, sacrum (`5` fused), coccyx (`4` fused). Cervical vertebrae have **transverse foramina**; C1 is the **atlas** (yes-nod), C2 the **axis** with its **dens** (no-shake). Thoracic vertebrae have costal facets for ribs and long downward spinous processes. Lumbar have thick blocky bodies for weight. Curves: cervical and lumbar are secondary (lordotic), thoracic and sacral are primary (kyphotic). Intervertebral discs are fibrocartilage with a nucleus pulposus inside an anulus fibrosus.

**Thoracic cage**: sternum (manubrium, body, xiphoid process; the **sternal angle** at the manubriosternal joint marks rib 2) and `12` pairs of ribs — `1–7` true (own costal cartilage to sternum), `8–10` false (shared cartilage), `11–12` floating.

## Appendicular skeleton

**Pectoral girdle**: clavicle and scapula. Scapular landmarks: spine, acromion, coracoid process, glenoid cavity. The girdle attaches to the axial skeleton at only one joint — the sternoclavicular — which buys mobility at the cost of stability.

**Upper limb**: humerus (head, greater and lesser tubercles, deltoid tuberosity, capitulum, trochlea, olecranon fossa, medial and lateral epicondyles), radius (lateral, thumb side; radial tuberosity, styloid process), ulna (medial; olecranon, coronoid process, trochlear notch), `8` carpals, `5` metacarpals, `14` phalanges.

**Pelvic girdle**: two coxal bones, each ilium plus ischium plus pubis, fused at the acetabulum. Landmarks: iliac crest, anterior superior iliac spine, ischial tuberosity (what you sit on), obturator foramen, pubic symphysis. Female pelvis is wider and shallower with a rounder inlet and a subpubic angle over `90` degrees.

**Lower limb**: femur (head, neck — the classic hip fracture site, greater and lesser trochanters, linea aspera, medial and lateral condyles), patella, tibia (medial, weight-bearing; tibial tuberosity, medial malleolus), fibula (lateral, non-weight-bearing; lateral malleolus), `7` tarsals (talus and calcaneus the big two), `5` metatarsals, `14` phalanges.

## Joints

Structural classification: **fibrous** (sutures, syndesmoses, gomphoses), **cartilaginous** (synchondrosis such as the epiphyseal plate, symphysis such as pubic symphysis and discs), **synovial** (joint cavity).

Functional: **synarthrosis** immovable, **amphiarthrosis** slightly movable, **diarthrosis** freely movable. All synovial joints are diarthroses.

A synovial joint has articular cartilage, a joint cavity, a capsule with synovial membrane, synovial fluid, ligaments, and nerves and vessels; some add bursae, menisci, or fat pads.

Six synovial types: **plane** (intercarpal), **hinge** (elbow, knee), **pivot** (atlantoaxial, proximal radioulnar), **condylar** (metacarpophalangeal), **saddle** (thumb carpometacarpal), **ball-and-socket** (shoulder, hip).

## Movements to name

Flexion and extension, hyperextension, abduction and adduction, circumduction, rotation. Special: **supination** (palm up) and **pronation** (palm down), **dorsiflexion** and **plantar flexion**, **inversion** and **eversion**, **protraction** and **retraction**, **elevation** and **depression**, **opposition** (thumb to fingertips).

> **Trap:** The shoulder trades stability for range and dislocates most often; the hip's deep acetabulum does the reverse.
keyPoints: 206 bones: 80 axial, 126 appendicular.
Radius is lateral (thumb side), ulna is medial; tibia is medial and weight-bearing, fibula is lateral and not.
C1 atlas nods yes, C2 axis with its dens turns no; cervical vertebrae have transverse foramina.
Ribs 1–7 true, 8–10 false, 11–12 floating; the sternal angle marks rib 2.
Six synovial joint types: plane, hinge, pivot, condylar, saddle, ball-and-socket.

checks.q: The pituitary gland sits in which landmark, and on which bone?
checks.why: The sella turcica is the saddle-shaped depression of the sphenoid. The foramen magnum passes the spinal cord and the cribriform plate passes olfactory fibers.

checks.q: Turning the palm from facing down to facing up is:
checks.why: Supination turns the palm upward, as if carrying soup. Pronation is the reverse; eversion is a foot movement.

checks.q: The thumb's carpometacarpal joint, which allows opposition, is which type of synovial joint?
checks.why: Saddle joints have reciprocally concave-convex surfaces that permit opposition. Hinge joints move in one plane only and ball-and-socket joints appear at the shoulder and hip.

lessons.title: Muscle: from sarcomere to named muscles
lessons.body:
## Organization

A whole muscle is wrapped in **epimysium**, divided into fascicles wrapped in **perimysium**, each fascicle full of muscle fibers (cells) wrapped in **endomysium**. Those sheaths merge into the **tendon**. Inside a fiber: **sarcolemma** (membrane), **sarcoplasmic reticulum** (stores calcium), **T tubules** (carry the impulse inward), and hundreds of **myofibrils** made of repeating **sarcomeres**.

## The sarcomere

Boundaries are **Z discs**. Thin filaments (**actin**, with **tropomyosin** and **troponin**) anchor to the Z disc. Thick filaments (**myosin**) sit in the middle. The **A band** is the full length of thick filament and never changes. The **I band** (thin only) and the **H zone** (thick only) both shrink during contraction, and so does the distance between Z discs.

> **Key:** On the exam, "which band does not change length during contraction?" is always the A band.

## The neuromuscular junction

A motor neuron ends at the motor end plate. The action potential opens voltage-gated calcium channels in the axon terminal, calcium triggers exocytosis of **acetylcholine (ACh)**, ACh crosses the synaptic cleft and binds nicotinic receptors, sodium rushes in, and an end plate potential becomes a muscle action potential. **Acetylcholinesterase** then chops ACh so the muscle can relax. Nerve agents and some pesticides block that enzyme, causing unrelenting contraction; curare blocks the receptor, causing paralysis; myasthenia gravis destroys the receptors, causing fatigable weakness.

## Excitation-contraction coupling and sliding filaments

The muscle action potential travels down the T tubules, the sarcoplasmic reticulum dumps `Ca2+`, calcium binds **troponin**, troponin drags **tropomyosin** off the myosin-binding sites on actin, and the cross-bridge cycle starts.

The cycle: myosin head (already cocked, carrying ADP and phosphate) binds actin, releases phosphate and pivots — the **power stroke** — then ATP binds and detaches the head, then ATP hydrolysis re-cocks it. Relaxation requires ATP too: calcium pumps run on ATP, and without ATP the heads stay bound, which is rigor mortis.

> **Trap:** The filaments never shorten. They slide past each other. The sarcomere shortens.

## Motor units and tension

A **motor unit** is one motor neuron and every fiber it innervates — a few fibers for the eye, over a thousand for the quadriceps. Tension rises by **recruitment** (adding motor units, smallest first) and by **wave summation** up to **tetanus** when stimuli arrive faster than the muscle can relax.

Contraction types: **isotonic concentric** (muscle shortens, lifting a weight), **isotonic eccentric** (muscle lengthens under load, lowering it — where most soreness comes from), **isometric** (tension without length change, holding a plank).

## Energy

Three systems, in order of speed: **creatine phosphate** (instant, `10–15` seconds), **anaerobic glycolysis** (fast, `30–60` seconds, `2` ATP per glucose, lactate accumulates), **aerobic respiration** (slow to start, unlimited while oxygen lasts, about `30–32` ATP per glucose). **Myoglobin** stores oxygen in the fiber. **Excess post-exercise oxygen consumption (oxygen debt)** repays creatine phosphate, glycogen, and oxygen stores afterward.

Fiber types: **slow oxidative** (type I, red, fatigue-resistant, postural muscles), **fast glycolytic** (type IIx, white, powerful, fatigues fast), and fast oxidative-glycolytic in between.

## Named muscles and how to think about them

Muscles are named by location (temporalis), shape (deltoid, trapezius), size (maximus, longus), direction of fibers (rectus, oblique, transversus), number of heads (biceps, triceps, quadriceps), or action (levator, flexor, extensor). Every action has an **agonist (prime mover)**, an **antagonist** that opposes it, **synergists** that assist, and a **fixator** that stabilizes the origin. The **origin** is the fixed attachment, the **insertion** the moving one.

| Muscle | Main action |
|---|---|
| Deltoid | Abducts the arm |
| Pectoralis major | Flexes and adducts, medially rotates the arm |
| Latissimus dorsi | Extends and adducts, medially rotates the arm |
| Biceps brachii | Flexes elbow, supinates forearm |
| Triceps brachii | Extends the elbow |
| Rectus abdominis | Flexes the vertebral column |
| Diaphragm | Primary muscle of inspiration |
| Gluteus maximus | Extends the hip |
| Quadriceps femoris | Extends the knee |
| Hamstrings | Flex the knee, extend the hip |
| Gastrocnemius | Plantar flexes the foot |
| Tibialis anterior | Dorsiflexes the foot |
keyPoints: Calcium binds troponin, moving tropomyosin off actin's binding sites — that is the switch for contraction.
ATP is required for both the power stroke reset and relaxation; its absence causes rigor mortis.
The A band never changes length; the I band and H zone shrink.
Tension rises by motor unit recruitment and wave summation to tetanus.
Energy order: creatine phosphate 10–15 s, anaerobic glycolysis 30–60 s, then aerobic respiration.

checks.q: Acetylcholinesterase is inhibited at the neuromuscular junction. The immediate result is:
choices: Flaccid paralysis from no ACh release
Loss of calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
checks.why: Without the enzyme, ACh stays in the cleft and keeps the end plate depolarized, so the muscle cannot relax. Curare, which blocks the receptor, is what causes flaccid paralysis.

checks.q: During contraction, which sarcomere region stays the same length?
checks.why: The A band equals the length of the thick filament, and filaments slide rather than shorten. I band, H zone and Z-to-Z distance all decrease.

checks.q: Lowering a heavy dumbbell slowly while the biceps lengthens under tension is:
checks.why: Eccentric contraction generates tension while the muscle lengthens, and it causes most delayed-onset soreness. Concentric shortens the muscle; isometric changes no length at all.

lessons.title: Nervous tissue, the action potential, and the synapse
lessons.body:
## Organization

The **central nervous system (CNS)** is brain and spinal cord. The **peripheral nervous system (PNS)** is everything else: cranial and spinal nerves, ganglia, receptors. Functionally the PNS splits into **sensory (afferent)** carrying signals in and **motor (efferent)** carrying signals out; motor splits into **somatic** (voluntary, skeletal muscle) and **autonomic** (involuntary, cardiac and smooth muscle, glands), and autonomic splits into sympathetic and parasympathetic.

## Neurons

A neuron has **dendrites** (receive), a **cell body (soma)** with the nucleus and Nissl bodies, an **axon** leaving at the **axon hillock** (where the action potential starts), and **axon terminals** that release neurotransmitter. Structurally, neurons are multipolar (most motor neurons and interneurons), bipolar (retina, olfactory), or unipolar/pseudounipolar (most sensory).

## Neuroglia

CNS: **astrocytes** (most numerous; blood-brain barrier, potassium and neurotransmitter cleanup), **oligodendrocytes** (myelinate, one cell wraps many axons), **microglia** (immune phagocytes), **ependymal cells** (line ventricles, make and circulate CSF). PNS: **Schwann cells** (myelinate, one cell per internode) and **satellite cells** (surround ganglion cell bodies).

Myelin is lipid insulation with gaps called **nodes of Ranvier**. The action potential jumps node to node — **saltatory conduction** — which is far faster than the continuous conduction of unmyelinated axons. Large diameter plus myelin equals fast; demyelination, as in multiple sclerosis, slows or blocks conduction.

## Resting state

Inside the neuron is about `-70 mV`. Potassium is high inside, sodium high outside, with the `Na+/K+` pump maintaining the difference and leak channels setting the voltage.

## Graded potentials versus action potentials

Graded potentials are small, variable in size, decay with distance, and can add up. If they push the axon hillock to **threshold** near `-55 mV`, an action potential fires.

The action potential is **all-or-none** and always the same size. Sequence:

1. **Depolarization**: voltage-gated sodium channels open, `Na+` rushes in, voltage races toward `+30 mV`. This is positive feedback.
2. **Repolarization**: sodium channels inactivate; voltage-gated potassium channels open and `K+` leaves.
3. **Hyperpolarization**: slow potassium channels overshoot past `-70 mV` before closing.
4. The `Na+/K+` pump restores the gradients over time.

Refractory periods matter: during the **absolute refractory period** no stimulus of any size can fire another impulse, because sodium channels are inactivated. During the **relative refractory period** a stronger-than-normal stimulus can.

> **Key:** Stimulus strength is coded by frequency of action potentials and by how many neurons fire, never by the size of a single action potential.

## The synapse

Electrical synapses use gap junctions and are instantaneous but rare. **Chemical synapses** dominate: the action potential reaches the terminal, voltage-gated `Ca2+` channels open, calcium triggers vesicle fusion, neurotransmitter diffuses across a `20–40 nm` cleft and binds postsynaptic receptors. Transmitter is then cleared by enzymatic breakdown, reuptake, or diffusion.

The result is an **EPSP** (excitatory, depolarizing, usually sodium in) or an **IPSP** (inhibitory, hyperpolarizing, usually chloride in or potassium out). The postsynaptic cell adds them up: **temporal summation** from one synapse firing rapidly, **spatial summation** from many synapses at once.

## Neurotransmitters worth naming

| Transmitter | Notes |
|---|---|
| Acetylcholine | Neuromuscular junction, all autonomic preganglionic, parasympathetic postganglionic |
| Norepinephrine | Most sympathetic postganglionic; mood and arousal |
| Dopamine | Reward, motor control; lost in Parkinson disease |
| Serotonin | Mood, sleep, appetite |
| GABA | Main CNS inhibitory transmitter |
| Glutamate | Main CNS excitatory transmitter |
| Endorphins | Natural opioid analgesia |

> **Trap:** A transmitter is not inherently excitatory or inhibitory. The receptor on the receiving cell decides. Acetylcholine excites skeletal muscle and slows the heart.
keyPoints: Resting potential about -70 mV, threshold about -55 mV, peak about +30 mV.
Sodium influx depolarizes, potassium efflux repolarizes, slow potassium channels cause hyperpolarization.
Action potentials are all-or-none; intensity is coded by frequency, not amplitude.
Saltatory conduction along myelinated axons jumps between nodes of Ranvier.
Whether a neurotransmitter excites or inhibits depends on the postsynaptic receptor.

checks.q: A toxin blocks voltage-gated sodium channels on an axon. What happens?
choices: Action potentials cannot depolarize past threshold
checks.why: Sodium influx is the depolarizing phase, so blocking it prevents the impulse entirely — the mechanism of local anesthetics. Blocking potassium channels would impair repolarization instead.

checks.q: Multiple sclerosis destroys myelin in the CNS. Conduction is slowed because:
choices: Axons lose their sodium channels entirely
Saltatory conduction is lost, so the impulse must travel continuously
The resting potential rises to zero
checks.why: Myelin lets the impulse jump between nodes; without it the axon must depolarize every patch of membrane, which is much slower. Transmitter release itself is not the primary defect.

checks.q: During the absolute refractory period, a very strong stimulus will:
choices: Produce no action potential at all
Produce a graded potential that reaches threshold
checks.why: Sodium channels are inactivated and cannot reopen regardless of stimulus strength. Only during the relative refractory period can a stronger stimulus succeed.

lessons.title: Brain, spinal cord, cranial nerves, autonomics, and the special senses
lessons.body:
## Brain regions

**Cerebrum**: two hemispheres of folded cortex (gyri, sulci, fissures) over white matter and deep basal nuclei. Lobes and jobs — **frontal** (primary motor cortex in the precentral gyrus, Broca area for speech production, judgment), **parietal** (primary somatosensory cortex in the postcentral gyrus), **temporal** (hearing, smell, Wernicke area for comprehension, memory via the nearby hippocampus), **occipital** (vision), **insula** (taste, visceral sense). The **corpus callosum** connects the hemispheres.

**Diencephalon**: **thalamus** relays every sensory input except smell to the cortex; **hypothalamus** is the homeostasis chief — temperature, thirst, hunger, circadian rhythm, autonomic control, pituitary control; **epithalamus** holds the pineal gland and melatonin.

**Brainstem**: **midbrain** (visual and auditory reflexes, substantia nigra), **pons** (bridge, helps control breathing rhythm), **medulla oblongata** (cardiac, vasomotor and respiratory centers, plus the decussation of the pyramids — the crossing that makes each hemisphere control the opposite side).

**Cerebellum**: coordination, balance, muscle tone, timing. Damage causes ataxia and intention tremor, not paralysis.

## Protection

Meninges from outside in: **dura mater**, **arachnoid mater**, **pia mater**; CSF flows in the subarachnoid space. **CSF** is made by choroid plexuses in the ventricles — about `500 mL/day` with `150 mL` circulating at any time — flows lateral ventricles to third to fourth ventricle, and is reabsorbed by arachnoid granulations. It cushions, floats the brain, and carries nutrients. The **blood-brain barrier** (tight junctions plus astrocyte feet) blocks most drugs but lets lipid-soluble molecules through.

## Spinal cord

Runs from the foramen magnum to about `L1–L2`, ending as the conus medullaris with the cauda equina below. Gray matter is central and butterfly-shaped (**posterior horns sensory, anterior horns motor**); white matter is outside in ascending and descending tracts. `31` pairs of spinal nerves: `8` cervical, `12` thoracic, `5` lumbar, `5` sacral, `1` coccygeal. Sensory fibers enter the **dorsal root** (with its dorsal root ganglion); motor fibers leave the **ventral root**. A **reflex arc** is receptor, sensory neuron, integration center, motor neuron, effector — the patellar reflex is monosynaptic, the withdrawal reflex is polysynaptic.

## Cranial nerves I–XII

| # | Name | Function |
|---|---|---|
| I | Olfactory | Smell (S) |
| II | Optic | Vision (S) |
| III | Oculomotor | Most eye movement, pupil constriction, lid (M) |
| IV | Trochlear | Superior oblique (M) |
| V | Trigeminal | Face sensation, chewing (B) |
| VI | Abducens | Lateral rectus (M) |
| VII | Facial | Facial expression, anterior tongue taste, tears and saliva (B) |
| VIII | Vestibulocochlear | Hearing and balance (S) |
| IX | Glossopharyngeal | Posterior tongue taste, swallowing, carotid baroreceptors (B) |
| X | Vagus | Parasympathetic to thorax and abdomen (B) |
| XI | Accessory | Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius (M) |
| XII | Hypoglossal | Tongue movement (M) |

## Autonomic nervous system

Two neurons in series with a ganglion between. **Sympathetic** is thoracolumbar (`T1–L2`), short preganglionic and long postganglionic fibers, chain ganglia near the cord, releases norepinephrine at the target: pupils dilate, heart rate and force up, bronchioles dilate, digestion down, glucose released, adrenal medulla dumps epinephrine. **Parasympathetic** is craniosacral (cranial nerves III, VII, IX, X and `S2–S4`), long preganglionic and short postganglionic, ganglia near the organ, releases acetylcholine: pupils constrict, heart slows, digestion and secretion up. Vagus alone carries roughly `75%` of parasympathetic output.

> **Trap:** Both divisions are active all the time. "Tone" is the balance between them, not an on-off switch.

## Special senses

**Eye**: three tunics — fibrous (sclera, cornea), vascular (choroid, ciliary body, iris), and inner (retina). Light passes cornea, aqueous humor, pupil, lens, vitreous humor, to the retina. **Rods** handle dim light and peripheral vision; **cones** handle color and detail and cluster in the **fovea centralis**. The optic disc has no photoreceptors and is the blind spot. The lens gets rounder for near objects when ciliary muscle contracts — **accommodation**. Myopia focuses in front of the retina (corrected by concave lenses), hyperopia behind it (convex lenses).

**Ear**: outer (auricle, external acoustic meatus, tympanic membrane), middle (malleus, incus, stapes; auditory tube to the pharynx), inner (cochlea for hearing with the organ of Corti and hair cells, plus the vestibule and three semicircular canals for equilibrium). High frequencies are detected at the base of the basilar membrane, low at the apex.

**Taste** uses five qualities — sweet, sour, salty, bitter, umami — via cranial nerves VII, IX, X. **Smell** uses olfactory receptors in the nasal roof whose axons pass the cribriform plate; it is the only sense that reaches the cortex without a thalamic relay.
keyPoints: Precentral gyrus is motor, postcentral gyrus is sensory; the medulla holds cardiac, vasomotor and respiratory centers.
Meninges outside in: dura, arachnoid, pia; CSF sits in the subarachnoid space, about 150 mL circulating.
Dorsal root is sensory, ventral root is motor; 31 pairs of spinal nerves.
Sympathetic is thoracolumbar and norepinephrine-releasing; parasympathetic is craniosacral and acetylcholine-releasing.
Rods are dim light and periphery, cones are color and detail at the fovea; smell bypasses the thalamus.

checks.q: A patient has fluent but meaningless speech and cannot understand what is said to them. Which area is damaged?
checks.why: Wernicke area handles comprehension, so damage yields fluent nonsense. Broca damage gives halting, effortful speech with preserved understanding.

checks.q: Which cranial nerve carries most parasympathetic output to the thoracic and abdominal organs?
checks.why: The vagus supplies about 75% of parasympathetic fibers, reaching heart, lungs and gut. Facial carries parasympathetic fibers only to tears and salivary glands.

checks.q: Sympathetic activation produces which combination?
choices: Pupil constriction, slowed heart, increased digestion
Pupil dilation, increased heart rate, bronchodilation
Pupil dilation, slowed heart, increased salivation
Bronchoconstriction, increased heart rate, glucose storage
checks.why: Sympathetic output prepares for exertion: dilate pupils, speed and strengthen the heart, open airways, shunt blood from gut to muscle. Constriction and digestion are parasympathetic.

cards.front: What are the three components of every homeostatic feedback loop?
cards.back: Receptor that senses the variable, control center that compares it to a set point, effector that changes it.

cards.front: Name three examples of positive feedback in the body.
cards.back: Oxytocin during labor, the platelet plug in clotting, and the sodium influx phase of an action potential. Each amplifies until an endpoint stops it.

cards.front: Which plane divides the body into anterior and posterior parts?
cards.back: The frontal (coronal) plane. Sagittal divides left from right; transverse divides superior from inferior.

cards.front: What is the difference between a parietal and a visceral serous membrane?
cards.back: Parietal lines the cavity wall; visceral covers the organ itself. Serous fluid between them reduces friction.

cards.front: Which abdominal structures are retroperitoneal?
cards.back: Kidneys, adrenal glands, pancreas, most of the duodenum, ascending and descending colon, abdominal aorta, inferior vena cava.

cards.front: What does anatomical position specify?
cards.back: Standing erect, feet forward and slightly apart, arms at the sides, palms facing forward. All directional terms assume it.

cards.front: What does the thoracic cavity contain besides the two pleural cavities?
cards.back: The mediastinum, which houses the pericardial cavity and heart, esophagus, trachea, great vessels and thymus.

cards.front: Which four elements make up about 96% of body mass?
cards.back: Oxygen about 65%, carbon 18%, hydrogen 10%, nitrogen 3%.

cards.front: What is the normal pH range of arterial blood, and what buffers it?
cards.back: 7.35 to 7.45, buffered mainly by the bicarbonate system: CO2 plus water gives carbonic acid, which gives H+ plus bicarbonate.

cards.front: How do dehydration synthesis and hydrolysis differ?
cards.back: Dehydration synthesis removes water to bond monomers into a polymer. Hydrolysis adds water to break a polymer apart, which is what digestion does.

cards.front: What are the four levels of protein structure?
cards.back: Primary is the amino acid sequence, secondary is the alpha helix or beta sheet held by hydrogen bonds, tertiary is the 3-D fold, quaternary is multiple chains joined.

cards.front: What does it mean to denature a protein, and what causes it?
cards.back: The three-dimensional fold unravels and function stops. Heat, extreme pH, or heavy metals cause it.

cards.front: How much energy do carbohydrates, proteins and fats yield per gram?
cards.back: Carbohydrate and protein 4 kcal/g each, fat 9 kcal/g.

cards.front: How does an enzyme speed a reaction?
cards.back: It lowers activation energy by holding substrate in its active site. It is not consumed, is substrate-specific, and is sensitive to pH and temperature.

cards.front: What ratio does the sodium-potassium pump move, and at what cost?
cards.back: Three Na+ out for every two K+ in, using one ATP. It is electrogenic and maintains the gradients other transport borrows.

cards.front: What is the typical resting membrane potential of a neuron, and what sets it?
cards.back: About -70 mV. Potassium leak channels outnumber sodium leak channels, trapped anionic proteins stay inside, and the Na+/K+ pump exports net positive charge.

cards.front: What happens to a cell placed in a hypertonic solution?
cards.back: Water leaves the cell and it shrinks, or crenates in the case of a red blood cell. Hypotonic solutions do the reverse and can lyse it.

cards.front: What percent saline is isotonic to human cells?
cards.back: 0.9% sodium chloride, normal saline. It causes no net water movement across the membrane.

cards.front: Which organelle makes proteins destined for secretion, and which ships them?
cards.back: Rough endoplasmic reticulum makes them; the Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts and packages them for exocytosis.

cards.front: Where do transcription and translation occur?
cards.back: Transcription is DNA to mRNA inside the nucleus. Translation is mRNA to protein on a ribosome in the cytoplasm or on rough ER.

cards.front: What are the start and stop codons?
cards.back: Start is AUG, which also codes methionine. Stops are UAA, UAG and UGA. Sixty-four codons encode twenty amino acids, so the code is redundant.

cards.front: What are the phases of interphase?
cards.back: G1 growth, S phase DNA replication, G2 preparation for division. Mitosis and cytokinesis follow.

cards.front: What five features define epithelial tissue?
cards.back: Cellularity with little matrix, polarity with apical and basal surfaces, attachment to a basement membrane, avascularity, and high regeneration.

cards.front: Which epithelium lines the trachea, and what does it do?
cards.back: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar with goblet cells. Cilia sweep mucus and trapped debris upward toward the pharynx.

cards.front: Which epithelium lines the urinary bladder and why?
cards.back: Transitional epithelium, or urothelium. Its cells change shape so the bladder can stretch and recoil without tearing.

cards.front: Name the three types of cartilage and one location for each.
cards.back: Hyaline at articular surfaces and costal cartilage, elastic in the ear and epiglottis, fibrocartilage in intervertebral discs and knee menisci.

cards.front: What is the difference between dense regular and dense irregular connective tissue?
cards.back: Dense regular has parallel collagen for one-direction pull, as in tendons and ligaments. Dense irregular has collagen in all directions, as in the reticular dermis.

cards.front: How do the three muscle tissue types differ in nuclei and striations?
cards.back: Skeletal is striated and multinucleate with peripheral nuclei, cardiac is striated with one or two central nuclei and intercalated discs, smooth is non-striated with a single central nucleus.

cards.front: Which tissue membrane has no epithelium at all?
cards.back: The synovial membrane lining joint cavities. It is connective tissue only, and it secretes synovial fluid.

cards.front: How do the three exocrine secretion modes differ?
cards.back: Merocrine exocytoses the product intact (sweat, pancreas), apocrine pinches off part of the cell apex, holocrine ruptures the whole cell (sebaceous glands).

cards.front: Name the epidermal strata from deep to superficial.
cards.back: Basale, spinosum, granulosum, lucidum (thick skin only), corneum. Mitosis happens in the basale.

cards.front: What are the four cell types of the epidermis?
cards.back: Keratinocytes make keratin, melanocytes make melanin, Langerhans (dendritic) cells are immune sentries, Merkel cells sense light touch.

cards.front: What are the two layers of the dermis?
cards.back: Papillary layer of loose areolar tissue with dermal papillae and capillaries, and the reticular layer of dense irregular connective tissue that provides strength.

cards.front: How do eccrine and apocrine sweat glands differ?
cards.back: Eccrine open onto skin nearly everywhere and make watery sweat for cooling. Apocrine open into follicles in the axilla and groin and begin at puberty.

cards.front: How does skin make vitamin D?
cards.back: UVB converts a cholesterol derivative in the epidermis to cholecalciferol, which the liver and then the kidney convert to active calcitriol.

cards.front: Give the adult rule of nines percentages.
cards.back: Head 9, each arm 9, each leg 18, anterior trunk 18, posterior trunk 18, perineum 1.

cards.front: Why is the center of a full thickness burn painless?
cards.back: The burn destroyed the dermis along with the sensory nerve endings in it. Lack of pain indicates greater depth, not a milder injury.

cards.front: What does ABCDE stand for in melanoma screening?
cards.back: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color variation, Diameter over 6 mm, Evolving appearance.

cards.front: What two materials give bone its mechanical properties?
cards.back: Collagen resists tension and gives flexibility; hydroxyapatite calcium phosphate resists compression and gives hardness.

cards.front: What are the four bone cell types and their jobs?
cards.back: Osteogenic cells are stem cells, osteoblasts build matrix, osteocytes maintain it and sense strain, osteoclasts resorb bone.

cards.front: Describe the structure of an osteon.
cards.back: Concentric lamellae around a central Haversian canal carrying vessels and nerves, with osteocytes in lacunae connected by canaliculi. Perforating canals link osteons crosswise.

cards.front: Which bones form by intramembranous ossification?
cards.back: Flat bones of the skull and the clavicle, which form directly within a fibrous membrane. Everything else forms by endochondral ossification from a hyaline cartilage model.

cards.front: What produces growth in bone length versus bone width?
cards.back: Length comes from the epiphyseal plate in the metaphysis. Width comes from appositional growth by periosteal osteoblasts.

cards.front: What does parathyroid hormone do to blood calcium, and how?
cards.back: Raises it. It activates osteoclasts, increases renal calcium reabsorption, increases phosphate excretion, and activates vitamin D to raise intestinal absorption.

cards.front: What is the normal serum calcium range, and why is it defended so tightly?
cards.back: About 9.0 to 10.5 mg/dL. Nerve excitability, muscle contraction, and clotting all depend on it; low calcium causes tetany.

cards.front: State Wolff's law and one consequence.
cards.back: Bone remodels along the lines of mechanical stress. Loaded bone thickens; bedrest or microgravity causes measurable bone loss.

cards.front: How many bones are in the adult skeleton, and how do they divide?
cards.back: 206 total: 80 axial (skull, hyoid, vertebral column, thoracic cage) and 126 appendicular (girdles and limbs).

cards.front: Name the eight cranial bones.
cards.back: Frontal, two parietal, two temporal, occipital, sphenoid, ethmoid.

cards.front: Which structure passes through the cribriform plate, and through the foramen magnum?
cards.back: Olfactory nerve fibers (cranial nerve I) pass the cribriform plate of the ethmoid. The spinal cord passes the foramen magnum of the occipital bone.

cards.front: How many vertebrae are in each region?
cards.back: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, sacrum from 5 fused, coccyx from about 4 fused — 26 bones in the adult column.

cards.front: Which ribs are true, false, and floating?
cards.back: Ribs 1 to 7 are true and attach to the sternum by their own costal cartilage, 8 to 10 are false and share cartilage, 11 and 12 are floating with no anterior attachment.

cards.front: Which forearm bone is lateral, and which leg bone bears weight?
cards.back: The radius is lateral, on the thumb side. The tibia is medial and bears weight; the fibula is lateral and does not.

cards.front: Name four landmarks of the scapula.
cards.back: Spine, acromion process, coracoid process, glenoid cavity where the humeral head articulates.

cards.front: Which three bones fuse to form each coxal bone, and where?
cards.back: Ilium, ischium and pubis, fusing at the acetabulum.

cards.front: List the six types of synovial joint with an example of each.
cards.back: Plane (intercarpal), hinge (elbow), pivot (atlantoaxial), condylar (knuckle), saddle (thumb carpometacarpal), ball-and-socket (shoulder and hip).

cards.front: Define supination, dorsiflexion and eversion.
cards.back: Supination turns the palm upward. Dorsiflexion lifts the toes toward the shin. Eversion turns the sole laterally, away from the midline.

cards.front: Name the three connective tissue sheaths of skeletal muscle from outside in.
cards.back: Epimysium around the whole muscle, perimysium around each fascicle, endomysium around each fiber. They converge to form the tendon.

cards.front: What is the trigger that exposes myosin binding sites on actin?
cards.back: Calcium binds troponin, which pulls tropomyosin off the binding sites. Calcium comes from the sarcoplasmic reticulum after the impulse travels the T tubules.

cards.front: What are the four steps of the cross-bridge cycle?
cards.back: Cocked myosin head binds actin, the power stroke pivots it as phosphate is released, ATP binds and detaches the head, ATP hydrolysis re-cocks it.

cards.front: Why does rigor mortis occur?
cards.back: ATP production stops, so myosin heads cannot detach from actin and calcium cannot be pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum. The muscle stays locked.

cards.front: Which sarcomere regions shorten during contraction, and which does not?
cards.back: The I band, the H zone and the Z-to-Z distance shorten. The A band does not, because it equals the fixed length of the thick filament.

cards.front: Which neurotransmitter acts at the neuromuscular junction, and what removes it?
cards.back: Acetylcholine, binding nicotinic receptors. Acetylcholinesterase in the cleft breaks it down so the muscle can relax.

cards.front: Compare the three muscle energy systems by duration and yield.
cards.back: Creatine phosphate gives about 10 to 15 seconds. Anaerobic glycolysis gives 30 to 60 seconds at 2 ATP per glucose. Aerobic respiration yields about 30 to 32 ATP per glucose.

cards.front: What is a motor unit, and how does recruitment change tension?
cards.back: One motor neuron plus all the fibers it innervates. Adding motor units, smallest first, increases whole-muscle tension smoothly.

cards.front: Which glial cell myelinates in the CNS, and which in the PNS?
cards.back: Oligodendrocytes in the CNS, each wrapping several axons. Schwann cells in the PNS, one cell per internode.

cards.front: Give the key voltages of a neuron: rest, threshold, peak.
cards.back: Rest about -70 mV, threshold about -55 mV, peak about +30 mV, then hyperpolarization below -70 mV before return.

cards.front: What ion movement causes depolarization and what causes repolarization?
cards.back: Sodium entering through voltage-gated channels depolarizes. Potassium leaving through voltage-gated channels repolarizes, then overshoots into hyperpolarization.

cards.front: What is saltatory conduction?
cards.back: The action potential regenerates only at nodes of Ranvier, appearing to jump between them along a myelinated axon. It is much faster than continuous conduction.

cards.front: How does a neuron code a stronger stimulus, if action potentials are all-or-none?
cards.back: By firing at a higher frequency and by recruiting more neurons. The amplitude of a single action potential never changes.

cards.front: How do temporal and spatial summation differ?
cards.back: Temporal summation adds rapid successive inputs from one synapse. Spatial summation adds simultaneous inputs from many synapses.

cards.front: Name the main excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitters of the CNS.
cards.back: Glutamate is the main excitatory transmitter; GABA is the main inhibitory transmitter.

cards.front: Which brain structure relays nearly all sensory input to the cortex, and what is the exception?
cards.back: The thalamus. Olfaction is the exception, reaching the cortex without a thalamic relay.

cards.front: What vital centers live in the medulla oblongata?
cards.back: Cardiac (rate and force), vasomotor (vessel diameter), and respiratory rhythm centers. The pyramids also decussate here.

cards.front: Name the meninges from outside in and where CSF flows.
cards.back: Dura mater, arachnoid mater, pia mater. CSF circulates in the subarachnoid space between arachnoid and pia.

cards.front: Where is CSF made and how much circulates?
cards.back: Choroid plexuses in the ventricles make about 500 mL per day; roughly 150 mL circulates at a time. Arachnoid granulations reabsorb it.

cards.front: Where does the spinal cord end, and what continues below it?
cards.back: It ends at about L1 to L2 as the conus medullaris; the cauda equina of lumbar and sacral roots continues below, which is why lumbar puncture is done at L3 to L4 or lower.

cards.front: Which spinal root is sensory and which is motor?
cards.back: The dorsal (posterior) root is sensory and has the dorsal root ganglion. The ventral (anterior) root is motor.

cards.front: Which cranial nerves are purely motor?
cards.back: III oculomotor, IV trochlear, VI abducens, XI accessory, XII hypoglossal. I, II and VIII are purely sensory; V, VII, IX and X are mixed.

cards.front: Where do sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers originate?
cards.back: Sympathetic is thoracolumbar, from T1 to L2. Parasympathetic is craniosacral, from cranial nerves III, VII, IX, X and spinal segments S2 to S4.

cards.front: How do rods and cones differ?
cards.back: Rods work in dim light, give no color, and dominate the periphery. Cones need bright light, give color and sharp detail, and pack the fovea centralis.

quiz.q: A student is asked to describe the position of the wrist relative to the elbow in anatomical position. The correct term is:
quiz.why: Proximal and distal apply to limbs and reference the point of attachment; the wrist is farther from the trunk, so it is distal. Proximal would be the reverse, and medial/superficial describe different axes entirely.

quiz.q: Body temperature rises during exercise, the hypothalamus detects it, and sweating and cutaneous vasodilation begin. This loop is:
choices: Negative feedback, because the response opposes the change
Positive feedback, because the response increases
Not feedback, because the stimulus is external
quiz.why: The response reverses the rise in temperature, which defines negative feedback. Positive feedback would drive temperature even higher, as in untreated malignant hyperthermia.

quiz.q: Inflammation of the membrane directly covering the surface of the lung involves which structure?
quiz.why: Visceral layers hug the organ; parietal layers line the cavity wall. Pericardium surrounds the heart and peritoneum the abdominal organs, so neither applies to the lung surface.

quiz.q: A solution has a pH of 5.0. Compared with a solution of pH 7.0, its hydrogen ion concentration is:
quiz.why: pH is a base-10 logarithmic scale, so each unit is a tenfold change and two units is 100-fold. A lower pH means more H+, not less.

quiz.q: A fever reaches 41 C and enzymes throughout the body begin to fail. The best explanation is that high temperature:
choices: Denatures proteins, disrupting active site shape
quiz.why: Heat breaks the weak bonds holding tertiary structure, so the active site no longer fits its substrate. ATP depletion and pH change are downstream effects, not the direct mechanism.

quiz.q: Which molecule class provides the most energy per gram and forms the structural basis of the plasma membrane?
quiz.why: Lipids yield 9 kcal/g and phospholipids form the bilayer. Carbohydrate and protein both yield 4 kcal/g, and nucleic acids store information rather than energy.

quiz.q: Cardiac glycosides inhibit the Na+/K+ ATPase. The immediate intracellular consequence is:
choices: The resting potential becomes more negative
quiz.why: The pump exports sodium, so blocking it traps sodium inside and lets potassium drift out. That reduces the sodium gradient, which secondarily reduces calcium export and makes the resting potential less negative.

quiz.q: Oxygen crosses the alveolar membrane into blood without a transporter or ATP. This is:
quiz.why: Oxygen is small and nonpolar, so it passes directly through the lipid bilayer down its gradient. Facilitated diffusion requires a protein and osmosis refers specifically to water.

quiz.q: A mutation changes one base so a codon reading UCU becomes UCC, and the same amino acid is still inserted. This is possible because:
choices: The genetic code is redundant, with several codons per amino acid
tRNA can carry any amino acid
Ribosomes proofread and correct the error
quiz.why: Sixty-four codons encode twenty amino acids, so most amino acids have multiple codons and third-base changes are often silent. Intron removal happens before translation and is unrelated.

quiz.q: A cell that secretes large amounts of steroid hormone would be expected to have abundant:
quiz.why: Smooth ER synthesizes lipids and steroids. Rough ER makes protein-based products, lysosomes digest, and microvilli increase absorptive surface.

quiz.q: A lab slide shows several layers of cells, flattened and keratin-filled at the free surface. This tissue is adapted for:
quiz.why: Stratified squamous keratinized epithelium is the wear surface of the epidermis. Diffusion and filtration require the single thin layer of simple squamous epithelium, and peristalsis is muscle.

quiz.q: Which tissue has abundant extracellular matrix with parallel bundles of collagen and few cells?
quiz.why: Parallel collagen resisting pull in one direction describes tendon and ligament. Areolar tissue is loose and irregular, and hyaline cartilage shows chondrocytes in lacunae within a glassy matrix.

quiz.q: After a myocardial infarction, the damaged heart wall is replaced by noncontractile scar. The reason is that cardiac muscle:
choices: Cannot meaningfully regenerate, so repair is by fibrosis
quiz.why: Cardiac muscle has almost no regenerative capacity, so collagen fills the defect and function is permanently lost. Cardiac muscle is in fact richly vascularized, which is why occlusion is so damaging.

quiz.q: Goblet cells and microvilli would most likely be found in which epithelium?
choices: Simple columnar of the small intestine
quiz.why: Absorptive intestinal lining combines microvilli for surface area with goblet cells for lubricating mucus. Alveolar and bladder linings have neither, and the esophagus is a protective wear surface.

quiz.q: Two people have visibly different skin tones. The physiologic difference is primarily:
choices: The thickness of the stratum corneum
The amount and type of melanin produced
quiz.why: Melanocyte number is roughly equal across populations; pigment output and melanin type differ. Corneum thickness varies by body region, not skin tone.

quiz.q: A burn victim has burns to the entire anterior trunk and one entire arm. Using the adult rule of nines, the estimated body surface area burned is:
quiz.why: Anterior trunk is 18% and a whole arm is 9%, totaling 27%. Adding the posterior trunk would reach 45%, and 18% alone omits the arm.

quiz.q: Which structure gives the skin its tensile strength and, when torn by rapid stretching, produces stretch marks?
quiz.why: The reticular layer is dense irregular connective tissue rich in collagen and elastin, and it is where the tearing occurs. The papillary layer carries capillaries and touch receptors instead.

quiz.q: Which skin cancer arises from cells of the stratum basale and is the most common but least likely to metastasize?
quiz.why: Basal cell carcinoma is most common and rarely spreads. Squamous cell carcinoma arises in the stratum spinosum and can metastasize; melanoma arises from melanocytes and is the most lethal.

quiz.q: A postmenopausal woman has reduced bone mass with normally mineralized matrix. This is:
quiz.why: Osteoporosis is a loss of bone quantity with normal composition, driven by osteoclast activity exceeding osteoblast activity. Osteomalacia and rickets are undermineralization of normal bone volume from vitamin D deficiency.

quiz.q: Which sequence correctly describes fracture repair?
choices: Bony callus, hematoma, soft callus, remodeling
Remodeling, hematoma, bony callus, soft callus
Soft callus, hematoma, remodeling, bony callus
Hematoma, fibrocartilaginous callus, bony callus, remodeling
quiz.why: Bleeding forms a hematoma first, then a soft fibrocartilaginous bridge, then a bony callus over roughly 6 to 8 weeks, then long-term remodeling. Repair cannot begin with callus or remodeling.

quiz.q: In compact bone, osteocytes exchange nutrients and signals with one another through:
quiz.why: Canaliculi are the tiny channels linking lacunae to each other and to the central canal. Central canals carry vessels, trabeculae are spongy bone struts, and Sharpey fibers anchor periosteum.

quiz.q: A patient's parathyroid glands are accidentally removed during thyroid surgery. Within a day you would expect:
choices: No change, because calcitonin compensates fully
Falling serum calcium with tetany and tingling
quiz.why: Without PTH, bone resorption, renal calcium retention, and vitamin D activation all fall, so calcium drops and nerves become hyperexcitable. Calcitonin lowers calcium further and cannot compensate.

quiz.q: Which vertebral feature is unique to cervical vertebrae?
quiz.why: Transverse foramina transmit the vertebral arteries and appear only in the cervical region. Costal facets mark thoracic vertebrae and thick blocky bodies mark lumbar ones.

quiz.q: Rotating the head to say no occurs mainly at which joint, and what type is it?
quiz.why: The dens of C2 acts as the pivot on which C1 rotates. The atlanto-occipital joint produces the nodding yes motion instead.

quiz.q: A fall on an outstretched hand fractures the bone on the thumb side of the forearm. Which bone is it?
quiz.why: The radius lies laterally, on the thumb side, and is the classic distal forearm fracture. The ulna is medial, on the little finger side.
