quiz.q: Which joint sacrifices stability for range of motion and is the most commonly dislocated in the body?
quiz.why: The shallow glenoid cavity permits huge range but little bony containment. The hip's deep acetabulum makes the opposite trade and dislocates only under major force.

quiz.q: The epiphyseal plate is classified structurally as which type of joint?
quiz.why: Hyaline cartilage uniting bone to bone without a cavity is a synchondrosis and is immovable. A symphysis uses fibrocartilage, and a syndesmosis uses a fibrous ligament.

quiz.q: Calcium released into the sarcoplasm binds directly to which protein?
quiz.why: Troponin is the calcium sensor; its shape change drags tropomyosin off actin's binding sites. Calcium does not bind actin or myosin directly.

quiz.q: A patient with myasthenia gravis has antibodies against acetylcholine receptors at the motor end plate. The expected finding is:
choices: Fatigable muscle weakness that worsens with use
Loss of sensation in the limbs
quiz.why: Fewer functioning receptors mean transmission fails as vesicle stores deplete, so weakness worsens through the day. Sustained contraction is the picture of acetylcholinesterase inhibition, the opposite problem.

quiz.q: A sprinter runs an all-out 200 meters. Which energy system supplies most ATP in the final seconds of that effort?
quiz.why: Creatine phosphate is exhausted by about 15 seconds, and aerobic metabolism cannot ramp fast enough, so glycolysis with lactate production carries the effort. Fat oxidation is far too slow for sprinting.

quiz.q: Which muscle is the prime mover of arm abduction, and which extends the elbow?
quiz.why: The deltoid abducts the arm and the triceps extends the elbow. Pectoralis major and latissimus dorsi both adduct, and the biceps and brachialis flex the elbow.

quiz.q: Stimuli arrive so rapidly that the muscle cannot relax between them and tension plateaus at maximum. This is:
quiz.why: Complete tetanus is fused, sustained maximal tension from stimuli outpacing relaxation. Recruitment adds motor units rather than stacking stimuli in time.

quiz.q: A local anesthetic such as lidocaine relieves pain because it:
choices: Blocks voltage-gated sodium channels, preventing action potentials
quiz.why: No sodium influx means the membrane never reaches threshold, so the pain signal never propagates. Blocking potassium channels would prolong action potentials rather than stop them.

quiz.q: Serum potassium rises from 4.0 to 7.0 mEq/L. Why does this destabilize excitable cells?
choices: The resting potential becomes more negative, so cells cannot fire
The potassium gradient shrinks, so the resting potential moves closer to threshold
quiz.why: Potassium leak sets the resting potential, so a smaller outward gradient depolarizes the membrane toward threshold and then inactivates sodium channels. It moves the resting potential less negative, not more.

quiz.q: Which glial cell forms the blood-brain barrier with the capillary endothelium and cleans up excess potassium?
quiz.why: Astrocytes wrap capillaries with end feet and manage the extracellular environment. Microglia are phagocytes, ependymal cells line the ventricles, and Schwann cells work only in the PNS.

quiz.q: An inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSP) is produced most often by:
choices: Chloride entering or potassium leaving the cell
quiz.why: Either movement makes the inside more negative, moving it away from threshold. Sodium and calcium entry both depolarize and would create an EPSP.

quiz.q: A patient after a stroke has weakness of the right arm and leg. The lesion is most likely in the:
choices: Right cerebral hemisphere, because of pyramidal decussation
Left cerebral hemisphere, because of pyramidal decussation
quiz.why: Corticospinal fibers cross in the medullary pyramids, so each hemisphere controls the opposite side. Cerebellar lesions cause same-side coordination loss rather than weakness, and lumbar cord cannot affect the arm.

quiz.q: Damage to the cerebellum most likely produces:
choices: Ataxia, intention tremor, and poor balance
quiz.why: The cerebellum times and smooths movement rather than initiating it, so damage gives uncoordinated movement with intact strength. Paralysis follows motor cortex or corticospinal tract injury.

quiz.q: A lumbar puncture is performed at the L3 to L4 interspace rather than higher because:
choices: The spinal cord ends near L1 to L2, leaving only the cauda equina below
CSF is produced only at that level
The vertebral bodies are fused above L3
quiz.why: Below the conus medullaris the needle meets floating nerve roots that move aside rather than solid cord. The dural sac actually continues to about S2, and CSF is made in the ventricles.

quiz.q: A patient cannot shrug the shoulders or turn the head against resistance. Which cranial nerve is affected?
quiz.why: The accessory nerve supplies the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid. The facial nerve moves the face, the vagus supplies viscera, and the hypoglossal moves the tongue.

scenarios.title: Lab practical walkthrough: station by station
scenarios.intro: It is the A&P I lab practical. Fifteen stations, ninety seconds each, a numbered pin in a specimen or model and a question card. No word bank. You will be asked to name a structure, state its tissue type, or give its function. Work the way the practical rewards: identify the region first, then the structure, then the answer they asked for.

steps.prompt: **Station 1.** A slide under the scope shows a single layer of flattened cells with bulging nuclei, forming the wall of a tiny sac. The card asks: name the tissue and state one location.

choices.text: Simple squamous epithelium; alveolus of the lung
choices.feedback: Correct. One layer plus flat cells equals simple squamous, and its job is diffusion — alveoli, capillary endothelium and serous membranes.

choices.text: Stratified squamous epithelium; epidermis
choices.feedback: The slide shows one layer, not many. Stratified squamous would look like a thick stack of cells flattening toward a free surface.

choices.text: Simple cuboidal epithelium; kidney tubule
choices.feedback: Cuboidal cells look like boxes with round central nuclei. These are flattened, so the answer is squamous.

choices.text: Transitional epithelium; bladder
choices.feedback: Transitional epithelium is multilayered with dome-shaped surface cells. A one-cell-thick wall rules it out.

steps.prompt: **Station 4.** A disarticulated bone sits on the tray: long, with a rounded head on a distinct neck, two large trochanters below, and two condyles at the far end. A pin sits in the neck. The card asks for the bone and the pinned landmark.

choices.text: Femur; neck of the femur
choices.feedback: Correct. Head, neck, greater and lesser trochanters, linea aspera, medial and lateral condyles — that is the femur, and the neck is the classic hip fracture site in older adults.

choices.text: Humerus; surgical neck
choices.feedback: The humerus has tubercles rather than trochanters, and its distal end shows a capitulum and trochlea, not two condyles of this size.

choices.text: Tibia; medial condyle
choices.feedback: The tibia has no head-and-neck arrangement and no trochanters. Its distinguishing landmarks are the tibial tuberosity and medial malleolus.

choices.text: Fibula; head of the fibula
choices.feedback: The fibula is thin, non-weight-bearing and has no trochanters. Size alone rules it out.

steps.prompt: **Station 7.** A muscle model: a large triangular muscle capping the shoulder, with fibers converging onto a tuberosity partway down the lateral humerus. The card asks for the muscle and its main action.

choices.text: Trapezius; elevates the scapula
choices.feedback: The trapezius is the large diamond on the back, attaching to the spine and skull. The muscle described caps the shoulder itself.

choices.text: Deltoid; abducts the arm
choices.feedback: Correct. Named for its triangular shape, inserting on the deltoid tuberosity, and it is the prime mover of arm abduction.

choices.text: Pectoralis major; abducts the arm
choices.feedback: Half right on naming and wrong on action. Pectoralis major is anterior on the chest and it adducts and medially rotates the arm.

choices.text: Latissimus dorsi; extends the arm
choices.feedback: Latissimus dorsi is a broad back muscle reaching the lumbar region. It does extend and adduct the arm, but it does not cap the shoulder.

steps.prompt: **Station 10.** A sheep brain, sagittally sectioned. The pin is in the thick band of white matter arcing above the thalamus and connecting the two hemispheres. The card asks for the structure and its function.

choices.text: Corpus callosum; connects the left and right cerebral hemispheres
choices.feedback: Correct. It is the largest commissure in the brain, and cutting it is what produces split-brain findings.

choices.text: Thalamus; relays sensory information
choices.feedback: The thalamus is the egg-shaped gray mass below the pin, not the white arc above it. Its relay function is right, but the location is wrong.

choices.text: Cerebellum; coordinates movement
choices.feedback: The cerebellum sits posterior and inferior, behind the brainstem, with its distinctive branching white matter.

choices.text: Pons; carries fibers to the cerebellum
choices.feedback: The pons is the bulge on the anterior brainstem, well below the thalamus.

steps.prompt: **Station 15, the free-response.** The card reads: *A student claims that during contraction the myosin and actin filaments themselves get shorter. Correct the statement and name the one sarcomere band that does not change length.*

choices.text: Filaments slide past one another rather than shortening; the A band stays the same length
choices.feedback: Correct on both counts. The A band equals the length of the thick filament, which never changes, while the I band, H zone and Z-to-Z distance all shrink.

choices.text: Filaments slide past one another; the I band stays the same length
choices.feedback: Right mechanism, wrong band. The I band is the thin-filament-only region and it shrinks as thin filaments are pulled inward.

choices.text: The student is correct; myosin coils up during the power stroke
choices.feedback: This is the single most common misconception in the unit. Myosin heads pivot, but filament lengths are fixed.

choices.text: Filaments slide past one another; the H zone stays the same length
choices.feedback: Right mechanism, wrong band. The H zone is the thick-filament-only gap and it narrows, sometimes disappearing, at full contraction.

scenarios.debrief: The practical rewards a fixed order of operations. First classify the specimen at the coarse level — slide, bone, muscle, or organ. Second, find the one landmark that eliminates everything else: trochanters mean femur, transverse foramina mean cervical, intercalated discs mean cardiac. Third, answer only the question asked. Most lost points come from naming the right structure and giving the wrong function, or from skipping the layer count on an epithelium slide. Train the two-part answer — name plus function — for every structure on the list.

scenarios.title: Exam question walkthrough: tracing a signal from nerve to movement
scenarios.intro: The lecture exam's final item is worth 20 points: *Trace the events from the arrival of an action potential at a motor neuron terminal to the shortening of the sarcomere, and predict what fails if ATP is absent.* You have ten minutes. Work the chain in order — no step may be skipped, and each named molecule earns a point.

steps.prompt: You start with the axon terminal. What is the first event once the action potential arrives there?

choices.text: Voltage-gated calcium channels open and calcium enters the terminal
choices.feedback: Correct. Calcium entry, not sodium, is the trigger for vesicle fusion at every chemical synapse.

choices.text: Acetylcholine diffuses across the cleft on its own
choices.feedback: That happens, but only after vesicles fuse. You skipped the calcium step, which is worth points.

choices.text: The sarcoplasmic reticulum releases calcium
choices.feedback: That is a later step, and it happens inside the muscle fiber, not the neuron. Keep the two calcium events separate.

steps.prompt: Acetylcholine has crossed the cleft and bound its receptors on the motor end plate. What happens next in the muscle fiber membrane?

choices.text: Sodium enters, an end plate potential forms, and a muscle action potential spreads along the sarcolemma and down the T tubules
choices.feedback: Correct. Naming the T tubules is what earns the point, because that is how a surface signal reaches the interior of a fiber tens of microns thick.

choices.text: Calcium enters through the acetylcholine receptor and binds troponin directly
choices.feedback: The nicotinic receptor is mainly a sodium channel, and calcium for contraction comes from internal stores, not the extracellular fluid.

choices.text: The muscle contracts immediately
choices.feedback: True but unscoreable. Exam prompts that say trace the events want the intermediate steps, not the endpoint.

steps.prompt: The impulse is deep in the T tubules. Describe excitation-contraction coupling.

choices.text: The sarcoplasmic reticulum releases calcium, calcium binds troponin, troponin moves tropomyosin off actin's myosin-binding sites
choices.feedback: Correct, and in the right order. Troponin is the receiver, tropomyosin is the cover being moved.

choices.text: Calcium binds tropomyosin, which pulls troponin aside
choices.feedback: The two are reversed. Calcium binds troponin; troponin then repositions tropomyosin. Graders mark this as a hard error.

choices.text: The sarcoplasmic reticulum releases calcium, which binds myosin heads and activates them
choices.feedback: Myosin heads are already cocked and ready. Calcium acts on the thin filament, not the thick one.

steps.prompt: Now the second half of the prompt: **predict what fails if ATP runs out.** Choose the fullest answer.

choices.text: Contraction stops immediately because the power stroke requires ATP hydrolysis at that moment
choices.feedback: Partly wrong on timing. The power stroke uses energy already stored in the cocked head; ATP binding is what releases the head afterward.

choices.text: Myosin heads cannot detach from actin and calcium cannot be pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, so the muscle stays locked — rigor mortis
choices.feedback: Correct and complete. Both the detachment step and the relaxation step are ATP-dependent, which is why death produces stiffness rather than limpness.

choices.text: The muscle goes limp because no cross-bridges can form
choices.feedback: This is the intuitive answer and the wrong one. Without ATP the bridges that already formed cannot let go.

steps.prompt: Last line of the answer. The question asks you to name the enzyme that ends the signal and what happens if it is inhibited.

choices.text: Acetylcholinesterase; inhibiting it leaves ACh in the cleft, causing sustained depolarization and continuous contraction
choices.feedback: Correct. This is the mechanism of organophosphate and nerve agent toxicity, and it is a favorite exam link.

choices.text: Acetylcholinesterase; inhibiting it causes flaccid paralysis
choices.feedback: Right enzyme, wrong consequence. Flaccid paralysis follows receptor blockade, as with curare, not enzyme inhibition.

choices.text: Choline acetyltransferase; inhibiting it stops the muscle from relaxing
choices.feedback: That enzyme synthesizes acetylcholine rather than degrading it, so blocking it would reduce transmission, not prolong it.

scenarios.debrief: Trace questions are graded as a chain, and every named molecule is a point: calcium at the terminal, acetylcholine in the cleft, sodium at the end plate, T tubules, sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium, troponin, tropomyosin, actin, myosin, ATP. Two reversals cost most students points — calcium binds troponin (not tropomyosin), and ATP is needed for detachment and relaxation (not for the power stroke itself). Memorize the chain in that order and write it as a numbered list on the exam so the grader can find each step.
